title: Devanagari
hook: every letter carries an a, yet the world ends on a t
tomorrow: should a beginner learn the script, or just use English letters?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari's short i: drawn before its letter, said after, read as one syllable. Today, a word that seems to break the rules.

Stop. Cut. Jet. English lets a word end hard, on a consonant, and nobody thinks twice. Devanagari has a problem with that. Every consonant carries a short a inside it: ka, not k; ta, not t. So how does a word end on a bare t? The Isha Upanishad's very first line ends on the word jagat, the world. Jagat, not jagata. On the page, the last letter is ta. Something has to switch its a off.
screen: `STOP. CUT. JET.` → `EVERY LETTER CARRIES AN A.` → `JAGAT, NOT JAGATA.`

segments.voice: Look under that last ta and there it is: a tiny slanted stroke, hanging below the letter like a kickstand. It's called the virama, a word for a stop, and it does exactly one job. It cancels the built-in a. Ta becomes t. Jagat ends where it should. The Isha's opening says, in paraphrase, that all this, whatever moves in the world, is to be dwelt in by the Lord. And the verse's world closes with that small stroke. Sanskrit needs the virama constantly, because so many words end on consonants: vak, speech; jagat, the world; the names of things that stop. Hindi often doesn't bother: it drops a final a in speech without writing anything, so a Hindi reader learns when to let it go quiet. Sanskrit is stricter. If the a isn't said, the page shows it. That's the solved puzzle, and it's a good one to keep. Devanagari would rather add a mark than leave the reader guessing. Where there's no mark, say the a. Where there's a virama, stop.
screen: `A STROKE UNDER THE LETTER.` · `THE VIRAMA CANCELS THE A.` · `HINDI OFTEN LETS IT GO QUIET.` · `NO MARK, SAY IT. VIRAMA, STOP.`

segments.voice: Say ja, ga, ta, slowly, giving each its a. Then say jagat, and let the last sound stop cleanly on the t, no vowel after it, and stay in the quiet right after the stop until the next breath comes. Do it once more on each out-breath: three soft syllables, then two, then the stillness.
Devanagari: a script where every consonant carries an a, and a small stroke, the virama, can switch it off.
Pocket this: Devanagari, where no mark means say the a, and a virama means stop cleanly. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sanskrit learners practice the virama by writing consonant-final words such as jagat and vak, and teachers listen for whether the final consonant is clipped cleanly rather than given an extra a.
